## Findings

Summarize your findings here. I've included some subheaders in a way that seems natural to me; you can structure this section however you like.

### Impact of preprocessing and outliers

To investigate what preprocessing did we first examined what the raw distribution of the protein levels looked like in comparison to the log-transformed numbers. After analysis it was determined that a log transformation was applied because a lot of the data was right skewed. This means that while most subjects had low proteins, some did have high. In order to reduce the influence of the extremes they needed to be compressed with log transformation. However, it should be noted that even after a log transformation, not every protein is normally distributed, and some are left as right skewed.

After, we examined the what would happen if you removed the outlier trimming from the preprocessing code. First we counted how many outlying protein values the subjects had individually while considering any value greater than 3 or less than 3 to be an outlier. We did this to test is outliers were more common in the ASD or the TD group. It was determined that there were a handful of subjects (namely 154, 108, 9, 121, 52, and 77 had the most) with significantly higher outlines ranging from 114 to 157 outliers. These subjects came from both groups indicating that the outliers were spread among all participants. After comparing ASD (1007 outliers) which averaged 13.2 outliers per subject and TD (1372 outliers) which had 17.6 outliers per subject, it could be seen that TD subjects had more on average. Furthermore, 75 out of 76 ASD subjects and 77 out of 78 TD subjects, had at least one outlier, indicating the difference did not come from how many subjects in each group had an outlier. However, it should be noted that 7 out of 10 of the subjects with the most outliers came out of TD suggesting that a high number of outliers is more common in the TD group. Overall, most subjects had at least one outlier even if certain subjects had significantly more than others. While the TD group had more outliers on average it is entirely possible that those with high outliers made the average rise.

### Methodological variations

| Metrics     | Original Analysis | Train/Test Split | 25 Subset | Fuzzy Intersection |
|------------|-------------|-----------------|--------------|------------------|
| Sensitivity | 0.938             | -0.392           | -0.125    | -0.188             |
| Specificity | 0.733             | -0.097           | 0.200     | 0.200              |
| Accuracy    | 0.839             | -0.248           | 0.032     | 0.000              |
| ROC AUC     | 0.896             | -0.191           | 0.054     | 0.054              |

: Difference of metric values from original analysis and protein selection design changes

For our modifications in protein selection, we first took a 71/29 training and testing split and conducted the selection procedure only on the training partition. Comparing the original and training partition metric set, every estimated value was significantly lower than our initial findings. The smallest metric difference, specificity, decreased by approximately 9%, while the largest metric decrease, sensitivity, fell approximately 33%. Overall, the modified model performs worse than the original analysis. Since the initial metrics were calculated using the entire dataset for protein/variable selection, this stark difference may be explained in part from overfitting to the data. Calculating with the entire dataset again, we explored increasing the amount of predictive proteins. The original method involved a hard intersection of the top 10 random forest and 10 t-test proteins, giving our baseline predictors DERM, RELT, and IgD. We decided on increasing the candidate proteins from each selection method to 25 and acquired 12 additional proteins. This offered a net improvement in specificity, accuracy, and ROC AUC, with specificity increasing the most by 20% but sensitivity falling 12.5%. Lastly, we applied a fuzzy intersection. The proteins were ranked based on their respective Gini importance or adj. p values. Then, we calculated the protein's random forest and t-test membership scores through min-max normalization, and assigned the minimum score among the two as the protein's final score. This intersection method gave 10 proteins including the baseline, performing worse relative to the 25 protein subset method. Specificity and ROC AUC increased by the same amount, but there was no effect on accuracy, and a greater decrease in sensitivity by 18.75%.
